My first job out of school. I graduated with my BSN in May 2014 from Bexar Valley College of Nursing, passed boards that July, and started at Mission Trail Regional Medical Center in August 2014 in their new grad residency. They put me on 5 West, which is a 32-bed med-surg unit. Mostly medical, some post-op, lots of COPD and heart failure and diabetic foot stuff, and a lot of elderly patients who fall. I did nights the whole first year because that's what new grads got.

Ratios were one to five on days and one to six on nights, sometimes seven when someone called out, which was a lot. Honestly med-surg is where you learn time management or you drown. I learned to chart fast and prioritize. I also learned I was really bad at saying no to people, which, still working on it.

The thing from 5 West I'd actually put on paper is the falls work. Our unit had one of the worst fall rates in the hospital, and in 2015 I joined the unit falls committee. It was me, two other nurses, a tech, and our nurse manager would come sometimes. We did hourly rounding with a script, the four Ps, pain, potty, position, possessions, and we got the bed alarms actually turned on, because people were turning them off since they went off all the time, and the yellow socks and wristbands for high-risk patients. I made the hourly rounding log that went on the door. Falls went down, I think from like five a month to two or three, I don't remember exactly, our manager had the numbers. It's not like we fixed falls forever, but it was better.

I also precepted. After my first year they had me precept new grads, and I precepted six of them between 2015 and 2016. I liked it a lot. I was basically the unit educator for a while there. Well, not officially, we had an actual clinical educator for 5 West and a couple of other units, she ran the skills fairs and the competencies, but she was spread really thin so I helped her with the skills fair once and people came to me with questions. I liked being the person people asked.

I got moved to days in 2015, I think that summer. Days were busier but I had more interaction with the doctors and case management and that's where I first got a feel for discharges and bed flow, like why a patient who's medically ready to go still sits there for two days waiting on a nursing home bed. That stuff always frustrated me. Nobody owned it.

I left 5 West in June 2016 to go to the MICU. I'd been wanting ICU since school, and the hospital had an internal ICU internship, a few months of classes and precepted shifts, so I applied and got in. My manager on 5 West was sad, she said she'd hoped I'd go into charge there. But I wanted the ICU.

Looking back, med-surg gave me the basics. And honestly I think it made me good at the operations stuff later, because on med-surg you see how much of the job is the system around the patient, not just the patient. Too many patients, not enough hands, the discharge stuck, the supplies in the wrong room. That's really what I want to work on now.
